old_title: Solheim Cup golf 2026: final day - Europe make flying start
new_title: Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe 15-13 USA - as it happened
old_text:
Auston Kim misses a short birdie putt on 4, and Lottie Woad, who had already converted, hits the front. Megan Khang shaves the cup on 11; so close to a bounceback birdie, but Charley Hull remains 2UP. And Celine Boutier leaves a birdie putt one roll short on 1, so no fast start for Europe in the anchor match. But Mimi Rhodes rattles in a 15-footer for birdie at 8 to halve the hole and hang on in there against Nelly Korda.

4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (9)

Par is enough to win the 6th hole for Nanna Madsen. Europe looking good at the top end of the scoreboard, but with so many players currently on terms, you'd be a brave soul to bet the farm on the outcome.

A third birdie of the day for the world number one Nelly Korda, this time at 7. She moves a couple up against Mimi Rhodes. Linn Grant and Angel Yin both make their birdie putts on 8, the latter snapping that dismal five-bogey streak. Charley Hull's two big hits into 10 prove enough to win the hole and double her lead over Megan Khang. Meanwhile Celine Boutier and Rose Zhang arrive on the 1st tee, and now all of the matches are out on the course.
Linn Grant cops a decent lie on a bald spot amid the heather down the right of 8. She takes advantage of her good fortune by wedging to eight feet. That turns the pressure up on Angel Yin, but she clips crisply out of the bunker to six feet. Putting contest coming up. Meanwhile Lottie Woad and Auston Kim trade birdies on 3, the former with an iron to four feet, the latter with a 20-foot putt. And on 4, Yealimi Noh and Julia Lopez Ramirez take turns to miss three-footers and the hole is somehow halved.
Angel Yin has made five bogeys in a row. But she's got the advantage on the short par-four 8th, finding the bunker guarding the front left of the green, Linn Grant flaying her tee shot towards heather down the right. Meanwhile up on the par-five 10th, Charley Hull hammers a fairway wood onto the front of the green to set up a long eagle chance. Her opponent Megan Khang is forced to lay up.
Having found water on 5, Angel Yin does it again on 7. Her ball in a creek guarding the front of the green. It costs her another hole. Julia Lopez Ramirez birdies 3 to level against Yealimi Noh. Meanwhile Nelly Korda drains a 25-footer on 6 to regain the lead against Mimi Rhodes.

4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (8)

It's going extremely well for Europe at the moment. Even a birdie for Yealimi Noh on 2, which gives her the lead against Julia Lopez Ramirez, doesn't change that. But the USA have started slowly in most of the disciplines so far, and managed to fight their way back on the later holes. There's a long way to go. It's still absolutely hosing down, by the way.
Birdie for Mimi Rhodes at 5, and the rookie has tied up her match against the world number one Nelly Korda! Another European rookie, Nastasia Nadaud, levels up against Andrea Lee, the latter having found that water. And so for a few seconds, there's no red on the board ... until Lauren Coughlin walks in a par putt on 1 to go up early doors against Leona Maguire. Meanwhile Alison Lee's antics down 7 hands another hole to Esther Henselit, as expected.

4UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (7)

Angel Yin misses the green at the par-three 6th, and it's another hole for Linn Grant. Her third in four holes. Yin's lack of competitive action catching up with her big-time. Alison Lee sends her third at 3 into a greenside bunker. And a messy double bogey by Nanna Madsen on 4 cuts her lead in half.
Not a good moment if your name is Lee. Alison's tee shot at 7 ends up under a tree atop some pine cones, and she's forced to punch out. Esther Henseleit finds the green in regulation and the US are in a spot of bother there. See also Andrea on 3, as her ball takes a flyer, whistling through the green and towards the water behind. She might have gone through the reeds and in, it's not clear from the pictures. Either way, it's not going to be good news for her.
Esther Henseleit becomes the first player today to go three holes up. Her tee shot at the par-three 6th finds the meat of the green; Alison Lee's effort bounds through and down the swale at the back. Lee can't get up and down, and par is enough for the German. Angel Yin's visit to the water on 5 costs her the hole and gifts Linn Grant the lead. But there's better news for the USA on 2, where Andrea Lee's birdie puts some red on the board.

3UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (6)

Woad v Kim
Angel Yin started fast, but having not played so much golf this year, the rust is beginning to show. She carves her third at 5 into the drink on the right. As if it isn't wet enough.
The rain is coming down in stair rods now. Players taking their shots as quickly as possible before scuttling back under the nearest umbrella. It's cold as well. In theory, these conditions should favour the Europeans, who will be more used to them ... but Angela Stanford sent her players out to practice under a deluge on Wednesday, and was at pains to emphasise that the US are prepared and ready to deal with wet weather. Thrills and spills ahoy!
Nanna Madsen looks to have benefitted from putting her feet up yesterday. She's now followed birdie at 1 with another at 2, and she's flown out of the traps. See also Esther Henseleit, who rolls in a 15-footer on 5 for birdie and Europe are 2UP in that match as well!

2UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (5)
Grant A/S Yin (4)
Rhodes v Korda 1UP (3)

Nastasia Nadaud and Andrea Lee take turns to shave the lip with mid-range birdie putts on 1. Up on 4, Angel Yin leaves a monster birdie effort a good ten feet short, and doesn't lose her turn. She can't make the par saver ... but Linn Grant spurns the opportunity to win the hole from five feet, her ball breaking away on the low side. Grant doesn't concede Yin's bogey putt, which to be fair looks well inside the leather. Gauntlet down, gloves off, Yin converts but doesn't look particularly happy about it. That may have been the entire point, of course.

Charley Hull has a reasonably straight six-footer on 5 for birdie and the win. But she leaves it up on the high side. Bit of a misread. An opportunity goes by. The rain is getting heavier.
Mimi Rhodes isn't close at 2. Nelly Korda is. Rhodes leaves a 50-foot putt ten short, but she doesn't get the opportunity to make par, because Korda steers in a gentle left-to-right curler from eight feet to hit the front in that match. Meanwhile bogey for Angel Yin at 3 gifts Linn Grant parity in match three.
1UP Hull v Khang (4)
1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (4)
Grant A/S Yin (3)
Rhodes v Korda 1UP (2)
1UP Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz (1)
Nadaud v An. Lee
Allisen Corpuz - in the bunker at the back of 1, having earlier been forced to chop out from the heather - has to hole out for the half. She can't do it. Europe go 1UP. Back on the tee, the latest match to go out is Andrea Lee versus the impressive rookie Nastasia Nadaud, the youngest player here this week. Two points in the bag for the 21-year-old French star-in-the-making already.
Charley Hull carves her tee shot at the par-three 4th into rough to the right of the green. But she nearly holes the chip up, and that's enough to scramble the half and retain her lead. Meanwhile on 1, Allisen Corpuz becomes the latest US player to find the bunker at the back of the green. Nanna Madsen nearly does the same, but her ball grabs the last bit of green and spins back to 12 feet. Advantage Europe in that one.
Mimi Rhodes very nearly drains a 30-footer on 1 for an early lead. But the ball stops one turn short. Not many putts racing past the hole so far. Not any. Back on the tee, Allisen Corpuz pulls her opening drive into the heather down the left. Her ball rears up and hits a marshal on the jacksie, a lovely cartoon touch. But back into the heather it disappears. From bracket to bracken. Nanna Madsen, freshly rested after a day off, splits the fairway. Meanwhile up on 2, Angel Yin spins her approach to kick-in range, and that's the first dash of red on the board this morning.
1UP Hull v Khang (3)
1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (2)
Grant v Yin 1UP (2)
Rhodes A/S Korda (1)
Koerstz Madsen v Corpuz
Alison Lee gets a bit of a flyer out of wet semi-rough down the right of 2. She doesn't get close to the flag, and though she lags her long birdie putt up to tap-in distance, Esther Henseleit has thrown a dart to six feet from the centre of the fairway and tidies up for birdie. Another splash of blue on the scoreboard. That putt only just dropped, though. The greens slow, to belabour the point.
1UP Hull v Khang (3)
1UP Henseleit v Al. Lee (2)
Grant A/S Yin (1)
Rhodes v Korda
The greens haven't run this slow all week: 10 on the stimp compared to 10.3 yesterday. And the players are struggling with the pace in these early matches. Angel Yin and Linn Grant become the latest to leave fairly straight birdie putts a couple of inches short on 1. Back on the tee, the world number one Nelly Korda prepares to face the rookie Mimi Rhodes, who already has two points in the bag for Europe this week. She's on record as saying she loves a challenge and the heat of battle; she's certainly got all of that on her plate today. They both find the wide, generous fairway.
1UP Hull v Khang (2)
Henseleit A/S Al. Lee (1)
Grant A/S Yin (1)
Rhodes v Korda
Charley Hull lets go of her club - a wet grip? - while sending her second at the par-five 2nd into a fairway bunker. She whips into the green and makes par, but Megan Khang set up a six-foot birdie chance to level the match. However she repeats the error of the 1st hole, leaving a dribbler short, failing to take into account the slowness of the wet greens. A let-off for Hull.
1UP Hull v Khang (2)
Henseleit A/S Al. Lee (1)
Grant v Yin
Angel Yin hasn't played too much golf recently - she's been ill earlier in the year, and sat out yesterday altogether - but displays no nerves in sending her opening drive down the middle. Linn Grant follows her. Up on the green, Alison Lee gets up and down from the bunker to salvage a half.
1UP Hull v Khang (1)
Henseleit A/S Al. Lee (1)
Grant v Yin
With the rain still coming down, and forecast to get heavier in the early afternoon, it's preferred lies today. Finding the fairway more important than ever. But you still have to take advantage. Esther Henseleit throws a dart at the flagstick on 1, her ball ten feet shy of the pin. But Alison Lee makes exactly the same mistake Megan Khang did, finding the bunker at the back. She's left with a slight downhill lie and not much green to play with. More good news for Europe coming up?
The US captain Angela Stanford references Jennifer Kupcho's heroics as she makes a bullish statement to Sky: "We needed a jolt ... they're all fired up this morning ... I'm pretty confident in the end of our line-up ... they're ready."
Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee take turns to split the fairway with their opening drives. Up on the green, Megan Khang doesn't give her five-footer enough oomph, the moisture on the green doing a number on her. The ball stays on the edge. The door open for Hull, and she walks on through. First blood to Europe!
Hull is further from the flag so will take her putt first. A 30-footer with some right-to-left swing. She leaves the putt three feet short, the morning rain having slowed the greens. Khang splashes out from the bunker to five feet. A couple of little testers coming up. Back on the tee, the second match of Esther Henseleit and Alison Lee arrives for work. Bedlam, bedlam, bedlam.
The adrenaline must be pumping ... and Megan Khang sends her approach through the green into a bunker at the back of 1. She can't believe it. "Long?!" she asks her caddie. It's long. Charley Hull responds with a slightly conservative play, finding the heart of the green, the pin tucked back left near Khang's bunker. But that's a slight advantage to Europe.
Here we go, then ... it's come to this. A rainy day at Bernardus Golf in Cromvoirt near Den Bosch in North Brabant, Netherlands. The gallery in good voice nonetheless. The first match of Charley Hull and Megan Khang receive the ovation they deserve. Both players have led their team out before, Khang beating Linn Grant in 2023, Hull seeing off Nelly Korda in 2024. That experience sees them good as they both pump fine drives down the track. No going back now!
It was a classic matchplay double whammy. An all-timer.Yesterday evening in the gloaming, with Europe looking likely to take a 9-7 lead into the Sunday singles, Jennifer Kupcho tramlined a 90-footer on 17 before guiding in a 30-footer on the last to pull the rug spectacularly, skilfully, nervelessly, dramatically from under the feet of the astonished hosts and level the scores at 8-8. A genuine Where Were You When ...? event, 120 feet's worth of brilliance you'll see again and again and again and again for ever more. And you can double that should the USA win and/or retain the trophy this afternoon! Take it to the bank. Jennifer Kupcho: instant Solheim Cup legend.
Can Europe recover from that late, late, great bodyblow? They've got 12 chances to do so. They need six-and-a-half more points to regain the Solheim Cup; the USA require a mere six to retain. If the first two days are anything to go by - and Carlota Ciganda's Seve-and-Spieth-infused heroics on Friday now seem a sepia-tinged dot in the dim and distant past in this post-Kupcho multicoloured world - this is going to be very tense, very dramatic ... and an awful lot of fun. It's on!

new_text:
It's time for every golf fan in Europe to concentrate on their celebrations - and not only that, but Ewan Murray's report from Bernardus has landed - so this blog must come to an end. Congratulations to Europe, commiserations to the USA ... and thank you, dear reader, for joining me, David Tindall and Matt Cooper for three days of top-drawer to-and-fro. Shall we all meet again for the 2028 edition at Valhalla? OK, it's a date!
... and so Team Europe comes up on to the stage, led by their captain Anna Nordqvist, who takes the crystal pot and hoists it high! Blue fireworks erupt in the background. On comes the music, as each player takes their turn to lift the trophy theatrically, the gallery hollering every time. Pure panto. Lovely.
Team USA are brought on to receive a warm ovation from the fans. Not too many smiling faces, understandably. But they're here to sportingly acknowledge the victors.
Team Europe are finally summoned to the tee. They're bouncing around in the manner you'd imagine. Carlota Ciganda busting some fine moves to her song, Seven Nation Army. Then they race off again, in a long snake, high-fiving everyone standing at the front of the gallery, plus all of the volunteers who have gathered around the tee. Everyone killing time as they wait interminably for the closing ceremony. Nobody minds.
It all started at the 1st tee on Friday morning ... and that's where it'll end tonight. Everyone packed into the stands surrounding the tee box, clapping and bopping to the music pumping, the presentation ceremony about to begin. All of Europe's players, some draped in the flags of England, Ireland, Spain, Denmark and Sweden, wait to be announced. They'll be lifting the cup in a minute or two.
The losing captain Angela Stanford, bitterly disappointed but still wearing a sporting smile, speaks to Sky Sports. "You hear people say how difficult it is ... and it really is ... we fought hard ... the Europeans played great today and that's how it goes ... good for them ... I try not to have regrets ... I believe in all 12 ... there are a lot of captains in line ... I think we have a lot lined up ready to go."
That was yet another magnificent Solheim Cup. Nip and tuck all the way to the end. Carlota Ciganda's channelling the walkabout spirit of her compatriot Severiano Ballesteros on Friday evening; Jennifer Kupcho making those putts heard around the world in the gloaming on Saturday; Charley Hull and Lottie Woad finally sprinkling their stardust on Sunday, before Ciganda saw off a Kupcho comeback to seal the deal. Marvellous entertainment. Europe the thoroughly deserved winners, but Team USA will be pleased with their performances too, once the pain of defeat eases off a bit. Every last player a hero.
3&2 Charley Hull v Megan Khang Esther Henseleit v Alison Lee 1UP 4&3 Linn Grant v Angel Yin Mimi Rhodes v Nelly Korda 4&2 2&1 Nanna Koerstz Madsen v Allisen Corpuz 3&2 Nastasia Nadaud v Andrea Lee 3&2 Julia López Ramírez v Yealimi Noh 2&1 Lottie Woad v Auston Kim Leona Maguire v Lauren Coughlin 2&1 Maja Stark v Lindy Duncan 3&1 4&2 Carlota Ciganda v Jennifer Kupcho Celine Boutier v Rose Zhang 2UP
The entire European team and their caddies advance up the 18th fairway linked arm in arm. Celine Boutier nearly drains a monster across the green for a birdie and that half she'd quite like ... but it doesn't drop. A wry smile as she concedes the hole to Rose Zhang ... then wanders off to celebrate with her pals! Rose Zhang beats Celine Boutier 2UP
The winning captain Anna Nordqvist - who heads into retirement as a Solheim Cup winning captain - speaks to Sky Sports. "This feels so good ... so much hard work ... all the background team ... we had a really good vibe all week ... everyone has been a really good team-mate ... we talked a lot about fast starts ... I'm really proud for them starting strong and finishing strong ... it's been such a long road ... I've been living my dream ... it doesn't feel like I've worked a day in my life ... what makes the Solheim Cup special is you get to share it with others ... thank you everyone!"
There's just one match left out on the course now. Rose Zhang is 1UP on Celine Boutier, having just won the 16th. Boutier will be desperate to win one of the last two holes, as she's the only player on the European team not to have contributed any points. I'm pretty sure her team-mates will say she was an integral part of a collective effort nonetheless. They'll have her back.
Maja Stark picks up Lindy Duncan's coin on the 17th green. The concession seals a fine win for the late-blooming rookie against one of Europe's grittiest competitors. Stark doesn't care. She just wants to race off and join the party with her team-mates. They all get in a huddle and bounce around singing her song. All together now: ♫ Maja Stark, doo doo doo doo doo doooo, doo doo doo doo doo doooo, doo doo doo doo doo doooo, MA-JA STARK! ♪♫ Lindy Duncan beat Maja Stark 3&1
Stark v Duncan 4&2 (F)
Boutier A/S Zhang (15) Europe 15-11 USA
Carlota Ciganda, who officially sealed the deal for Europe, talks to Sky. "I am so happy ... we had a great team all week ... very happy for Anna ... you need a team, that's what Europe is about ... we had a great time ... Kupcho is a fighter ... I know I celebrated yesterday and probably pissed off all the Americans! ... I was really motivated to beat her!"
What a difference a day makes. Yesterday evening, Jennifer Kupcho drained putts of 92 feet and 30 feet on 17 and 18. Now she underhits a putt from the swale to the right of 16, the ball only just getting to the green. Carlota Ciganda nearly drains her eagle putt, but she doesn't need to make the one coming back, because Kupcho's long birdie effort races past the hole, and the American concedes. Europe have officially won the 2026 Solheim Cup! Carlota Ciganda beats Jennifer Kupcho 4&2
Stark v Duncan 2UP (16)
4&2 Ciganda v Kupcho (F)
Boutier A/S Zhang (15) Europe 15-11 USA
Lauren Coughlin and Leona Maguire half 17 in par, and that's a belated point on the board for the USA. Not that it really matters. Lauren Coughlin beats Leona Maguire 2&1
Maguire v Coughlin 2&1 (F)
Stark v Duncan 2UP (16)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (15)
Boutier A/S Zhang (15) Europe 14-11 USA
... but Europe haven't officially won, because Carlota Ciganda has to complete her match to register the half-point she's certain of posting. She finds the heart of 16 in two, while her opponent Jennifer Kupcho misses to the right. No ear cupping today from Kupcho. It's not been the smartest of moves by either Kupcho or Auston Kim in retrospect ... but then if you can't celebrate wildly after making 122-feet's worth of putts, when can you? So having said all of the above: the celebration police can do one. Kupcho will always have Saturday night.
Europe win the Solheim Cup (effectively, if not officially)!
Lottie Woad's win sparks huge celebrations on the 17th green! Anna Nordqvist comes over to give the hero of the hour a huge hug, before Sky have a word with the brilliant 22-year-old from Farnham in Surrey! "I didn't know it was to win ... I thought Carlota's match was to win ... I was playing good golf but not getting the points ... I felt I was kinda letting everyone down ... then the captain spoke to me ... said I was third on birdies ... I had to trust that ... that's golf sometimes and I get the winning putt!"
Auston Kim's putt shaves the left-hand edge of the cup. She hangs her head. She knows the jig is up, though she makes Lottie Woad tap in to seal the deal. With Carlota Ciganda assured of half a point, Woad has effectively won the Solheim Cup for Europe! Lottie Woad beats Auston Kim 2&1
2&1 Woad v Kim (F)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (16)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (15)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (14)
Boutier A/S Zhang (13) Europe 14-10 USA
Lauren Coughlin with a huge display of grit on 16, getting up and down to scramble par having found the drink. That secures a half, and puts her dormie two. Meanwhile up on 17, Lottie Woad and Auston Kim both find the green in regulation. Woad has a look at birdie from 25 feet, but it's always dying to the right. Kim will have a chance to extend if she makes her birdie effort from 15 feet or so. She'll have got a read off Woad too. But she needs to make it, because if not, the cup is effectively Europe's (although not officially, because matches have to be completed before counting).
2UP Woad v Kim (16)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (16)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (15)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (14)
Boutier A/S Zhang (13) Europe 13-10 USA
Jennifer Kupcho doesn't put a good stroke on her birdie putt. The ball jumps a little as it rolls wide right. That gives Carlota Ciganda the chance to put this match to bed ... but her putt is always staying up on the left. The hole halved, and Ciganda is dormie three. Europe are now guaranteed to reach 14 points, which means they can't lose the 2026 Solheim Cup ... but they need to get to 14-and-a-half, because the USA as holders have the tie.
2UP Woad v Kim (16)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (15)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (15)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (14)
Boutier A/S Zhang (13) Europe 13-10 USA
Lauren Coughlin's second into 16 finds the drink. So nothing's signed and sealed just yet. Leona Maguire whistles her second long and right of the green. Much will depend on her lie. Meanwhile both Carlota Ciganda and Jennifer Kupcho are on the 15th green, with similar looks at birdie. Kupcho perhaps a bit further out, but as we saw last night on 17 and 18, distance is not exactly an issue for her.
Auston Kim bundles her chip up to 12 feet, but she's outside Lottie Woad ... and can't make the par putt. That leaves Woad with two putts to win the hole from ten feet ... and she only needs one. She tickles it in, and goes dormie two. Europe are guaranteed half a point now, so if Carlota Ciganda can hold onto her lead over Jennifer Kupcho ... and having just halved 14, she's 3UP with four to play ... the Solheim Cup will be heading back to Europe! But last night's shenanigans proved there's many a slip twixt cup and lip ...
2UP Woad v Kim (16)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (15)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (15)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (14)
Boutier A/S Zhang (11) Europe 13-10 USA
Woad eases her wedge over the flag on 16. She'll have a good look at birdie, with Kim in trouble to the right of the green in three. Meanwhile back on the par-three 15th, two matches come through in short order, Lauren Coughlan and Lindy Duncan missing putts to win the hole, and in Duncan's case her match. Duncan now dormie three over Maja Stark.
1UP Woad v Kim (15)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (15)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (15)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (13)
Boutier A/S Zhang (11) Europe 13-10 USA
Auston Kim may have gone a little early with those ear-cupping antics. She carves her tee shot at the par-five 16th into the drink ... and then having taken her drop, sprays her third into rough to the right of the green. Lottie Woad meanwhile has laid up in front of the creek in two.
Yealimi Noh's 15-foot birdie putt is always staying up on the high side. That opens the door for Julia Lopez Ramirez to win the match with her four-foot birdie putt ... and she walks through it with a firm, confident roll! Cue wild celebrations, the rookie seeing off one of the US's most accomplished performers. Julia Lopez Ramirez beats Yealimi Noh 3&2
3&2 Lopez Ramirez v Noh (F)
1UP Woad v Kim (15)
Maguire v Coughlin 2UP (14)
Stark v Duncan 3UP (14)
3UP Ciganda v Kupcho (13)
Boutier A/S Zhang (11) Europe 13-10 USA
Carlota Ciganda walks in a 35-footer on 13 to get back to 3UP against Jennifer Kupcho, who was halfway through her comeback. Big momentum shift! Maja Stark makes a 20-footer on 14 to keep her slim hopes alive against Lindy Duncan. And on 16, Yealimi Noh, having laid up, doesn't get particularly close with her wedge ... and then Julia Lopez Ramirez races her eagle putt six past! Both of these players have really suffered with the old greenside nerves in the last 30 minutes or so.
Lottie Woad gives her birdie putt an aggressive run, and with her ball ending up three feet past, it's not conceded. Woad takes her time and eventually tickles it in for the half. She remains 1UP. Meanwhile Leona Maguire isn't giving up. Two putts for the hole on 14, and she takes them carefully, reducing Lauren Coughlin's lead to two holes. ops: It's time for every golf fan in Europe to concentrate on their celebrations - and not only that, but Ewan Murray's report from Bernardus has landed - so this blog must come to an end. Congratulations to Europe, commiserations to the USA ... and thank you, dear reader, for joining me, David Tindall and Matt Cooper for three days of top-drawer to-and-fro. Shall we all meet again for the 2028 edition at Valhalla? OK, it's
date! ... and so Team Europe comes up

to the stage, led by their captain Anna Nordqvist, who takes the crystal pot and hoists it high! Blue fireworks erupt in the background. On comes the music, as each player takes their turn to lift the trophy theatrically, the gallery hollering every time. Pure panto. Lovely. Team USA are brought on to receive a warm ovation from the fans. Not too many smiling faces, understandably. But they're here to sportingly acknowledge the victors. Team Europe are finally summoned to the tee. They're bouncing around in the manner you'd imagine. Carlota Ciganda busting some fine moves to her song, Seven Nation Army. Then they race off again, in a long snake, high-fiving everyone standing at the front of the gallery, plus all of the volunteers who have gathered around the tee. Everyone killing time as they wait interminably for the closing ceremony. Nobody minds. It all started at the 1st tee on Friday morning ... and that's where it'll end tonight. Everyone packed into the stands surrounding the tee box, clapping and bopping to the music pumping, the presentation ceremony about to begin. All of Europe's players, some draped in the flags of England, Ireland, Spain, Denmark and Sweden, wait to be announced. They'll be lifting the cup in a minute or two. The losing captain Angela Stanford, bitterly disappointed but still wearing a sporting smile, speaks to Sky Sports. "You hear people say how difficult it is ... and it really is ... we fought hard ... the Europeans played great today and that's how it goes ... good for them ... I try not to have regrets ... I believe in all 12 ... there are a lot of captains in line ... I think we have a lot lined up ready to go." That was yet another magnificent Solheim Cup. Nip and tuck all the way to the end. Carlota Ciganda's channelling the walkabout spirit of her compatriot Severiano Ballesteros on Friday evening; Jennifer Kupcho making those putts heard around the world in the gloaming on Saturday; Charley Hull
Woad, who had already converted, hits
Woad finally sprinkling their stardust on Sunday, before Ciganda saw off a Kupcho comeback to seal

deal. Marvellous entertainment. Europe the thoroughly deserved winners, but Team USA will be pleased with their performances too, once the pain of defeat eases off a bit. Every last player a hero. 3&2 Charley Hull v

Charley Hull responds with a slightly conservative play, finding the heart of the green, the pin tucked back left near Khang's bunker. But that's a slight advantage to Europe. Here we go, then ... it's come to this. A rainy day at Bernardus Golf in Cromvoirt near Den Bosch in North Brabant, Netherlands. The gallery in good voice nonetheless. The first match of Charley Hull and Megan Khang receive the ovation they deserve. Both players have led their team out before, Khang beating Linn Grant in 2023, Hull seeing off Nelly Korda in 2024. That experience sees them good as they both pump fine drives down the track. No going back now! It was a classic matchplay double whammy. An all-timer.Yesterday evening in the gloaming, with Europe looking likely to take a 9-7 lead into the Sunday singles, Jennifer Kupcho tramlined a 90-footer on 17 before guiding in a 30-footer on the last to pull the rug spectacularly, skilfully, nervelessly, dramatically from under the feet of the astonished hosts and level the scores at 8-8. A genuine Where Were You When ...? event, 120 feet's worth of brilliance you'll see again and again and again and again for ever more. And you can double that should the USA win and/or retain the trophy this afternoon! Take it to the bank. Jennifer Kupcho: instant Solheim Cup legend. Can Europe recover from that late, late, great bodyblow? They've got 12 chances to do so. They need six-and-a-half more points to regain the Solheim Cup; the USA require a mere six to retain. If the first two days are anything to go by - and Carlota Ciganda's Seve-and-Spieth-infused heroics on Friday now seem a sepia-tinged dot in the dim and distant past in this post-Kupcho multicoloured world - this is going to be very tense, very dramatic ... and an awful lot of fun.
